strengths: The environment is well engineered: end-to-end JAX vectorization with dynamic, JIT-free reconfiguration of unit specifications, zones, heuristic policies, and physics parameters at reset time is a genuine practical advantage over SMAX/JaxMARL, which require recompilation for new scenarios; the throughput comparison (Fig. 10) explicitly accounting for JIT overhead on scenario resets makes this advantage concrete and quantified.

The paper demonstrates a broad and coherent set of use cases: MARL benchmarking (Fig. 4), controlled analysis of centralized value learning via value-estimation error against Monte Carlo reference values (Fig. 5), sparse-reward exploration with RND (Fig. 7, plus a useful hyperparameter sensitivity grid in Fig. 28), and multi-agent UED with DR/PLR/PLR⊥/ACCEL/SFL (Fig. 8, 31, 32) — the UED integration in particular leverages the environment's key differentiator.

Reproducibility is treated seriously: full hyperparameter tables, hardware/software stack details, wall-clock training times for every baseline, scenario specifications with screenshots, and an extensive appendix documenting observation structure, action space, physics, reward design, and heuristic policy mechanisms.

The role-appropriate heuristic policy (Assassin/Ranger/Healer behavioral primitives with difficulty tiers) is a thoughtful addition beyond the typically homogeneous scripted opponents in prior battle benchmarks, and the asymmetric bush-visibility mechanics introduce a genuinely interesting dynamic-POMDP element.

Presentation quality is generally good, with clear figures, an intuitive GUI editor (Figs. 2, 14–17), and a well-organized compositional scenario naming scheme that supports systematic generalization studies.
weaknesses: Originality is modest. TABX is fundamentally a battle arena in the SMAC/SMAX lineage with JAX acceleration; the core contribution is incremental engineering (parameterized reset, GUI editor, terrain zones) layered on an established environment template. The comparison in Table 1 uses criteria that favor TABX (e.g., 'configurable params' judged as ✓ vs △ for competing frameworks) and the evaluation is somewhat self-serving.

The scientific findings from the analysis experiments are largely confirmatory rather than novel: centralized critics help when global state is necessary and not otherwise (consistent with De Witt et al., 2020, which the authors acknowledge), RND helps sparse-reward exploration (expected from Burda et al., 2019), and replay-based UED methods underperform DR on unit-specification shifts is the only mildly surprising observation, and even that is offered with a speculative explanation rather than analysis.

The claim that TABX features 'significantly augment the strategic complexity of the task' is asserted but not rigorously validated — no comparison of sample complexity or emergent behavior against an equivalent simpler environment to show the added primitives create qualitatively different strategic demands rather than just more difficulty.

The code availability statement is effectively empty ('Our code is available at:' with no URL on page 1 and in Appendix A), which undercuts the reproducibility claims central to a resource paper; at submission time the artifact cannot be verified.

Polish issues reduce confidence: Fig. 10's legend labels the proposed environment 'TABS' rather than 'TABX'; inconsistent lists of free-parameter categories ('two categories... unit specifications and zones' vs. a later list of three); grammatical errors ('performs strongly than IQL', 'useable'); and some results (e.g., ribbon/grid win rates below 0.1 after 30M steps in Fig. 4) suggest the benchmark may be too hard for its own baseline suite, with only a single extended-horizon run (Fig. 27) partially addressing this.

The scalability study is limited to a comparison against SMAX on random-policy throughput; no end-to-end training-time comparison, no CPU-vs-GPU analysis beyond a brief mention, and throughput claims at 10^8–10^9 steps/sec (Fig. 9 axis) are for random policies with no learning in the loop, which overstates practical training throughput.

strengths: The engineering effort is substantial: TABX provides a GPU-accelerated, end-to-end JAX implementation with demonstrated throughput scaling (Figures 9-10), dynamic reconfiguration of unit specifications and zone layouts without JIT recompilation, and a graphical scenario editor (Figures 2, 14) that lowers the barrier to scenario authoring.

The experimental program is broad and organized around concrete research questions: MARL baselines across eight scenarios (Figure 4), a value-estimation-error analysis of centralized critics (Figure 5), sparse-reward exploration with RND (Figure 7), a UED/zero-shot generalization study with DR, PLR, PLR⊥, ACCEL, and SFL (Figure 8), and useful wall-clock time reporting (Tables 9-11).

The hyperparameter and implementation details in Appendices D-F are fairly thorough, and the scenario documentation (Appendix C) makes the experimental conditions explicit; results are averaged over five seeds with standard error regions.

The observation that UED baselines generalize well to zone-layout variation but poorly to unit-specification variation (Section 5.5) is a somewhat interesting empirical observation that existing spatially-focused benchmarks could not easily produce.
weaknesses: Reproducibility, the core promise of an environment paper, is undermined: the code URL is literally missing in both the abstract ('Our code is available at:') and Appendix A. For a paper whose central contribution is a released tool, an empty link is a decisive flaw, and the text even claims 'The implementations used in our experiments are made available to support reproducibility' without an artifact to point to.

Originality is limited. TABX is a close sibling of SMAX within JaxMARL (Rutherford et al., 2024b) and OGC (Ruhdorfer et al., 2025): a configurable battle/cooperation environment with parameterized opponents and layouts. The Table 1 comparison asserts TABX uniquely offers full configurability, but the claimed contrast (e.g., SMAX as 'code-level', JaxNav/OGC with '△' configurable params) is asserted rather than substantiated, and the paper's stated delta over these systems (terrain zones, unit attributes, dynamic reset) reads as incremental feature additions rather than a new capability class.

The scientific findings are largely confirmatory of prior results. The IPPO vs. MAPPO observation (Section 5.2) explicitly restates De Witt et al. (2020), and the QMIX > IQL finding restates well-known properties of monotonic value factorization. The centralized-critic analysis (Section 5.3) is also somewhat circular: scenarios were hand-designed with an expected outcome ('a controlled setting where centralized value learning is expected to provide little to no advantage'), so the experiment largely validates the design intent rather than producing new insight.

The value error analysis (Section E.3) is methodologically thin: V* is estimated via only 128 Monte Carlo rollouts per state under the current policy, which is a high-variance approximation, yet the paper draws strong conclusions ('centralized value learning achieves substantially lower estimation error') from this noisy proxy without confidence quantification.

Presentation quality is below the bar: several broken or redundant sentences (e.g., 'Nevertheless, given that both tasks require high-level exploration..., suggesting that...' is a fragment; duplicated statement that 'movement actions are defined in a global coordinate frame' in A.2; 'performs strongly than' in 5.2), inconsistent naming between TABX and 'TABS' (Figure 10 legend, GUI header 'TABS Scenario Editor'), a garbled Figure 5 axis label, and redundant 'Future Work' heading formatting.

Key claims are under-supported: 'TABX exhibits significant sample complexity' (Section 5.2) is asserted without any comparison to baseline difficulty in existing benchmarks; the potential explanation for DR outperforming replay-based UED methods under unit-specification shift (Section 5.5) is speculative and untested; the UED results are aggregated over a small hand-constructed level space (four training compositions, six zone primitives), which limits how general the generalization conclusions are.

No dedicated limitations discussion: the paper acknowledges missing capabilities only in future work (no line-of-sight obstacles, no pixel observations), but does not honestly discuss limitations such as dependence on hand-crafted heuristic opponents for difficulty calibration, the small scale of the UED level space, or the absence of any human-/usability-based validation of the claimed GUI benefit.

strengths: TABX is a well-engineered, end-to-end JAX environment combining GPU acceleration, dynamic reconfiguration of unit/terrain/heuristic/physics parameters without recompilation, and an intuitive GUI scenario editor — a combination that Table 1 shows is genuinely not offered by existing MARL benchmarks (e.g., SMAX, JaxMARL, GrF).

The experimental design is organized around explicit research questions rather than leaderboard-style results: scenarios are deliberately constructed to probe centralized value learning (Figure 5 value-estimation error is a nice, quantified analysis), sparse-reward exploration, and zero-shot generalization over two independent parameter axes (unit specs vs. zone layouts).

Reproducibility is treated seriously: full observation/action/reward specifications, unit statistics, heuristic policy parameters, hyperparameter tables for all baselines, hardware/software versions, and even wall-clock training times are provided.

The scalability study (Figures 9-10) including JIT-compilation overhead at re-instantiation is the right metric for the paper's core claim about frequent scenario reconfiguration, and the demonstrated throughput advantage over SMAX supports it.

The zero-shot generalization finding (robust to zone-layout shifts but poor transfer across unit specifications) is a genuinely interesting, non-obvious empirical observation that the framework uniquely enables.

Detailed mechanics (hurtbox geometry, collision resolution, bush-zone visibility rules, asymmetric tie-breaking in the reward) are documented to a level that supports independent reuse and replication.
weaknesses: Scientific novelty is limited: the core contribution is an engineering effort combining existing ingredients (JAX vectorization from JaxMARL/SMAX-style environments, battle mechanics from SMAC/MPE-style games, UED support from JaxUED). The paper's findings largely confirm prior knowledge (centralized critics help when state is essential; RND/entropy trade-offs in sparse rewards) rather than producing new understanding beyond the unit-vs-zone generalization asymmetry.

The throughput claim ('high-throughput') is only quantified against SMAX. Comparisons against other JAX-accelerated MARL environments (JaxMARL SMAC-type tasks, OG-Gym) on equal hardware would substantially strengthen the scalability claims; without them, Table 1's positioning is partly assertion.

Baseline coverage is narrow: four MARL algorithms (two policy-gradient, two value-based) and standard UED methods, all integrated with MAPPO. Given the paper's pitch as a systematic evaluation platform, results with more diverse algorithm families (e.g., transformation-based value factorization, communication methods) would better demonstrate discriminative power.

Several evaluation choices are opaque or weakly justified: V* is approximated via Monte Carlo rollouts under the current policy (fine, but then Figure 5 compares MAPPO vs. IPPO only — value-based methods are omitted), the number of pretrained opponents/scenarios behind Figure 10 is modest, and why the UED study initializes opponents with a novice-level policy while MARL benchmarks use a medium-level policy deserves more justification.

Presentation issues remain: the code URL in the abstract and Section A is apparently blank/placeholder ('Our code is available at:'), which is a direct reproducibility concern; there are copy-editing errors ('performs strongly than'); and the sheer volume of appendix figures/tables suggests the paper would benefit from consolidating the scenario taxonomy.

The environment remains restricted to fixed-topology, entity-based combat with elliptical zones; the authors themselves note missing obstacle occlusion and pixel observations. This limits claims of broad 'sandbox' generality relative to the abstract's language.

No discussion of how sensitive the reported algorithm rankings are to reward shaping choices (dense health-difference reward plus terminal ±1); the asymmetric tie-breaking rule is sensible but its effect on the conclusions is not ablated.

strengths: Clear and genuine gap identification: existing MARL battle benchmarks (SMAC/SMACv2, SMAX) are static and require code modification or JIT recompilation to reconfigure scenarios, and TABX addresses this with recompilation-free, fully parameterized resets — a well-motivated and practically useful contribution (Sections 1, 2, 5.6, Figures 9-10).

Substantial engineering and thorough system documentation: the environment, observation/state/action spaces, physics, reward, unit statistics, zones, and heuristic policies are described in detail (Sections 4, A.1-A.8, Tables 2-3), and the GUI scenario editor (Section B, Figures 14-17) lowers the barrier for scenario authoring.

The experimental program is unusually comprehensive for a benchmark paper: MARL baselines across eight scenarios (Section 5.2), a controlled analysis of centralized vs. independent value learning tied to scenario structure (Section 5.3, Figure 5, correlation analysis in Section G), exploration studies with RND and hyperparameter sweeps (Sections 5.4, J.3, Figure 32), a multi-agent UED/zero-shot generalization study (Section 5.5), policy-vs-policy evaluation (Section I), and scalability comparisons against SMAX.

commendably honest self-assessment: the fixed-configuration throughput comparison (Section H, Figure 26) shows TABX can be slower than SMAX for large teams, and the authors correctly attribute their advantage to recompilation-free resets rather than faster simulation; the Limitations section (Section 6) candidly states the experiments are 'primarily illustrative'. The impact statement thoughtfully addresses the combat-framing concern.

The UED finding that unit-specification variation is a qualitatively distinct and harder generalization axis than zone/layout variation (Section 5.5, Figures 8, 33-36), with the health-attribute ablation, is a reasonably interesting empirical observation enabled by the environment's design.
weaknesses: The code URL is blank in the manuscript ('Our code is available at:' appears on pages 1 and 13 with no link), which undermines the reproducibility claims that are central to a benchmark/environment paper. Given that the entire contribution is the artifact, this is a significant presentation and reproducibility weakness that must be fixed.

The core scientific findings are largely confirmatory or preliminary: IPPO vs. MAPPO asymmetries echo prior findings (De Witt et al., 2020), and the authors themselves concede the experiments 'do not yet yield fundamentally new insights into MARL algorithms' (Section 6). The value-error analysis (Section 5.3) has modest absolute gaps and relies on a post-hoc Pearson correlation (r = -0.82) across only 8 scenario-level points, which is a fragile evidential basis for the claimed causal link between value error and performance.

The claim that scenarios 'isolate' specific variables (e.g., clover/ribbon requiring global state) is asserted by design intuition rather than validated: no experiment directly measures the informational content of local vs. global observations, and the scenario-level confounds (unit compositions, rewards, geometry) are not disentangled. The MAPPO>IPPO gap in clover/ribbon could have alternative explanations.

The Related Work comparison (Table 1) is self-serving and partially unfair: entries like MiniGrid, Craftax, and Kinetix are single-agent by design yet are used to rank TABX favorably, and the 'configurable params' column judgments appear subjective without defined criteria.

Several methodological details are under-specified or inconsistent: JAX version 'v0.6.1+' appears not to exist (Section E), training budgets are stated inconsistently (5e7 vs 2e7 vs 1e8 vs 3e7 steps across Sections E and J.6 with different GPUs/CPUs), and Figure 4/5 x-axes appear inconsistent with stated training budgets; wall-clock tables (J.6) use different hardware than the scalability experiments, complicating interpretation.

The narrative claim of 'qualitatively different learning dynamics' versus SMAX (Sections 2.1, D, Figure 21) rests on only three matched scenarios with two algorithms and heuristically aligned dynamics; the alignment procedure itself (matching unit specifications and action dynamics 'as closely as possible') introduces confounds and is not fully specified.

Only 5 seeds with standard-error shading are used for most claims; given the high variance visible in several curves (e.g., encirclement in Figure 7, grid in Figure 4), stronger statistical treatment (e.g., IQM/rliable as the paper itself cites Agarwal et al., 2021) would be expected for the headline comparisons.

strengths: The environment is technically well-executed: a fully JAX-based, end-to-end vectorized battle simulator with recompilation-free scenario resets is a real practical advance over SMAX/JaxMARL, and the throughput analysis (Figures 9, 10, 26) honestly isolates where the speed advantage comes from (eliminating JIT recompilation) rather than claiming raw per-step superiority.

The experimental suite is broad and reasonably rigorous for a benchmark paper: four MARL baselines across eight scenarios, five seeds with standard error, a value-estimation error analysis with a Monte Carlo reference (Figure 5, correlation analysis in Section G), RND-based exploration studies, UED baselines (DR/PLR/PLR⊥/ACCEL/SFL), and policy-vs-policy payoff matrices.

The zero-shot generalization study yields the most interesting scientific finding of the paper: UED methods generalize well over terrain zones but fail on unit-specification variation (win rates below 50%), with health identified as the dominant bottleneck via isolated ablations. This suggests a genuine gap in multi-agent UED.

Reproducibility is treated seriously: hyperparameter tables, wall-clock times, detailed environment mechanics (hurtbox geometry, collision resolution, reward structure, heuristic policy tiers), scenario specifications, and a GUI editor are all documented. The limitations section is candid, including the admission that experiments are 'primarily illustrative'.
The impact statement appropriately contextualizes the combat framing and discourages military interpretation.
weaknesses: Limited originality relative to prior art: the core contribution is largely an incremental composition of existing ingredients — JaxMARL-style JAX environments, SMAX-style battle scenarios, config-based parameterization (as in Kinetix), and UED integration (JaxUED). The Table 1 comparison is somewhat self-serving; the 'high-dimensional parameter space' claim reduces in practice to passing a config dict at reset.

The paper's own limitation section concedes that the experiments 'do not yet yield fundamentally new insights into MARL algorithms.' The findings are mostly confirmatory (IPPO vs MAPPO depends on partial observability structure; QMIX > IQL is consistent with known inductive biases; RND helps in sparse-reward tasks). For an ICML main-track paper, the environment would need to enable at least one robust, novel, method-level insight beyond the UED-under-unit-variation observation.

The central scientific analyses rest on thin evidence: the centralized-vs-independent value learning claim (Section 5.3) is supported by only four hand-crafted scenarios and five seeds, and the 'informational dependence' of scenarios is asserted by design rather than validated independently. The correlation analysis (r = -0.82) conflates scenario-level confounds — scenarios designed to be harder are exactly those with larger value error.

The UED generalization conclusion is drawn from four training scenarios and a small, hand-specified evaluation suite (Table 4). Alternative explanations — e.g., reward-scale coupling with health values, or distributional range choices for unit specifications — are not controlled for, making the 'health is the bottleneck' attribution under-supported.

Comparison to SMAX on matched scenarios (Appendix D) is described qualitatively ('qualitatively different learning dynamics') without a principled way to determine whether differences stem from richer dynamics or from unintentionally mismatched difficulty tuning; the heuristic opponent calibration is not validated against human or expert play.

Some inconsistencies and loose writing reduce polish: e.g., 'kitting' vs 'kiting', the claim of 'orthogonal' role classes that are simultaneously stated to be non-mutually exclusive, and the misplaced Background section on UED that plays little role in the main narrative.

Practical significance is uncertain: the paper does not address community adoption questions (rendering/pixel observations are deferred to future work, no standard leaderboard, no reference to integration with existing MARL algorithm libraries beyond the authors' own baselines), which limits near-term usefulness as a benchmark.

strengths: TABX is a well-engineered, genuinely useful contribution: the combination of end-to-end JAX vectorization, recompilation-free scenario reconfiguration, a rich parameter space (unit specs, terrain zones, heuristic opponents, physics), and a GUI scenario editor addresses a real gap in configurable MARL benchmarking, as motivated in Table 1.

The experimental program is unusually thorough for a benchmark paper: baseline sweeps across eight scenarios (Fig. 4), a targeted analysis of centralized vs. independent value learning (Sec. 5.3, Fig. 5), sparse-reward exploration with RND and entropy ablations (Fig. 7, Fig. 32), a multi-agent UED study with DR/PLR/PLR⊥/ACCEL/SFL (Fig. 8, Figs. 33-36), policy-vs-policy payoff matrices (Fig. 27), and careful throughput comparisons against SMAX that separately isolate recompilation overhead from per-step simulation cost (Figs. 10, 26).

The UED finding that unit-level parameter variation is a qualitatively harder generalization axis than spatial/zone variation, with health identified as the dominant bottleneck, is a genuinely interesting empirical insight enabled by the environment's design (Sec. 5.5).

Reproducibility is strong: code is promised, detailed environment mechanics (obs/state/action/reward/physics/zone rules) are specified in Appendix A, full hyperparameter tables are provided, and wall-clock training times are reported. The matched-scenario comparison with SMAX (Appendix D) strengthens the claim that TABX induces distinct learning dynamics rather than just re-implementation.

The limitations section is honest (combat-only scope, illustrative rather than novel algorithmic findings), and the impact statement carefully addresses potential misinterpretation of a combat-themed simulator.
weaknesses: The scientific insights, while carefully constructed, are largely confirmatory: the MAPPO/IPPO/QMIX/IQL ordering patterns, the centralized-critic dependence on global-state structure, and RND helping in sparse-reward settings largely re-derive known results in a new environment. The paper's own limitations section concedes the experiments 'do not yet yield fundamentally new insights into MARL algorithms.'

The central quantitative claim in Sec. 5.3 rests on a correlation computed over only eight scenario-level points (r = -0.82, p = 0.0128, n = 8), which is fragile evidence; the value-error gaps in Fig. 5 are themselves modest and the paper leans on discounting arguments to explain their significance.

Internal inconsistencies undermine polish and reproducibility: Table 9 states MARL agents trained for 2×10^7 steps while the main text (Sec. E) states 5×10^7; wall-clock experiments use an RTX PRO 6000/Xeon 6767P while the throughput benchmarks use an RTX 4090/Threadripper; there are typos ('performs strongly than', 'kitting', 'Enviornment', duplicated sentence in A.2).

The claimed differentiation of scenarios by global-state dependence (e.g., crossfire/vsrangers vs. clover/ribbon) is supported by design rationale and outcome patterns, but no direct measurement or causal manipulation of the information structure is provided, so the interpretation remains partly qualitative.

Several baseline results show large overlaps across five seeds (e.g., Fig. 4, Fig. 8), and no rigorous statistical testing (e.g., rliable-style IQM comparisons, following the cited Agarwal et al. 2021) is applied to the comparative claims, despite the paper citing that work in its motivation.

Novelty over existing configurable frameworks (SMAX/JaxMARL, OGC, Kinetix) is incremental in mechanism; the main differentiators are breadth of parameterization and the GUI editor, which is engineering-heavy rather than methodologically novel.
